title: Lattice Health - SLA/SLO + incident comms review (Dedicated/Private readiness)
summary: Lattice Health security/compliance team reviewed Redwood’s reliability commitments for a Dedicated deployment: how internal SLOs map to contractual SLAs, what incident communications look like (status page vs direct notifications), and what evidence Redwood can provide that reliability controls are enforced (error budgets, burn-rate alerting, release freeze gates, post-incident follow-ups). Redwood clarified SLI/SLO definitions (availability vs streaming disconnects; exclusions), tier-specific comms expectations, and provided a plan to share the SLO/SLA mapping doc plus a sample error-budget report and incident update templates.
topics: SLO vs SLA definitions and mapping for Hosted vs Dedicated
SLI measurement boundaries (gateway vs routing; end-to-end latency; streaming disconnect accounting)
Error budget policy: burn-rate alerting, breach thresholds, and enforcement (warn-only → hard gates)
Incident communications: timelines, channels, and tier-specific status messaging
Evidence package for compliance: dashboards, policy docs, postmortems, auditability
questions: If we buy Dedicated, what exact SLA language do we get and what’s excluded (client aborts, invalid requests, rate limits)?
How do you count streaming failures—are disconnects treated like 5xx? What about client-side aborts?
How do we know you actually enforce error budgets (release freeze, rollback expectations) and it’s not just a dashboard?
What is your incident notification timeline and do you send account-specific comms for Dedicated?
Can you provide an example monthly SLO/error budget report and evidence for audits?
next_steps: Redwood to share internal/external-facing SLO↔SLA mapping draft for Dedicated (definitions + exclusions) (owner: Elliot Price).
Redwood to send tiered status communications guidelines + sample incident update templates (owner: Rachel Kim).
Redwood to provide a redacted example of an error budget burn summary + screenshot walkthrough of tiered dashboards (owner: Aisha Bello).
Customer to confirm target regions + top 2 critical endpoints (chat vs embeddings) for initial SLO targets and reporting format (owner: Miguel Alvarez).
Schedule a follow-up technical deep dive on dedicated routing/fallback behavior and how it impacts SLI accounting (owner: Markus Klein).

transcript:
Fireflies.ai meeting transcript

Title: Lattice Health - SLA/SLO + incident comms review (Dedicated/Private readiness)
Date/time: 2026-02-05 08:00 PT (16:00 UTC)
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees:
- Markus Klein (Redwood, Solutions Engineering)
- Rachel Kim (Redwood, CS Enterprise)
- Aisha Bello (Redwood, Senior SRE)
- Elliot Price (Redwood, Customer-facing documentation)
- Dana Patel (Lattice Health, Security & Risk)
- Tom Nguyen (Lattice Health, Compliance)
- Sarah Keane (Lattice Health, Legal)
- Miguel Alvarez (Lattice Health, Platform Engineering)
- Priya Sood (Lattice Health, Procurement)

---
Summary (auto-generated)
Lattice asked how Redwood’s internal tiered SLO program connects to contractual SLAs, what counts against availability/latency/streaming reliability, and what comms and evidence Redwood can provide for audits. Redwood explained SLI measurement (tier tagging at ingress, exclusions), error budget enforcement (burn-rate alerts, release gates, incident triggers), and tier-specific communication practices.

---
[00:00] Markus Klein: Alright, thanks everybody for making time. This is mostly a review of how we do SLOs, how that maps to SLAs for Dedicated, and then incident communications—what you can expect and what we can prove, basically.

[00:19] Dana Patel: Yep. For us it’s not just “say you have an SLA.” We have to show we have vendor controls. So we need something we can hand to our audit team. Evidence, not marketing.

[00:32] Rachel Kim: Totally understood. We’re seeing more of that, especially in regulated workflows. We can cover both: contractual language and operational process.

[00:41] Sarah Keane: I’m going to be annoying and very literal. If you say “99.9,” I want: measurement window, exclusions, remedies, and incident notice obligations.

[00:52] Elliot Price: That’s helpful. We have a mapping doc that ties the engineered SLO definitions to customer-facing SLA terms. It also spells out exclusions like invalid requests.

[01:04] Miguel Alvarez: And from engineering, I want to know where you measure. Like at the gateway, after routing, at the model server. Because that changes what we see.

[01:15] Aisha Bello: Great question. We can walk through the SLI boundaries. The intent is end-to-end from the API gateway receiving the request to the response completion, with tier tags preserved through routing and fallback. There are some nuances with streaming.

[01:34] Markus Klein: Maybe let’s do quick agenda: (1) Hosted vs Dedicated tiers and what commitments differ, (2) SLI/SLO definition basics, (3) error budgets and enforcement, (4) incident comms, and then (5) what artifacts we’ll send.

[01:52] Dana Patel: Works.

[02:00] Sarah Keane: Fine.

[02:02] Markus Klein: Cool. So first, deployment. You’re looking at Dedicated, right? Potentially Private later.

[02:09] Miguel Alvarez: Dedicated in your cloud region, ideally US-East + EU. Private is “maybe,” but not in phase 1.

[02:17] Markus Klein: That matches what we’ve seen. For Dedicated, we treat it as reserved capacity—isolated GPU pools and predictable throughput. Hosted is shared.

[02:28] Tom Nguyen: For compliance, do you do data residency by region? Like EU stays in EU.

[02:34] Markus Klein: For Dedicated, yes, region pinning is part of the config. We can cover retention separately, but from reliability: the SLOs are tracked per region.

[02:45] Aisha Bello: And the tier is a first-class label at ingress. We don’t want “oh, it got routed to X so now it’s measured as Hosted.” Tier follows the request.

[02:56] Miguel Alvarez: So you tag at the gateway?

[02:58] Aisha Bello: Correct. At the API gateway, based on the customer/account and deployment mode. That’s to avoid ambiguity downstream.

[03:10] Dana Patel: That’s good, because we’ve had vendors who “can’t tell” what tier a request was, and the reporting is useless.

[03:20] Markus Klein: Right. Ok, SLAs vs SLOs. So internally we have SLO targets per tier. Externally you’d get an SLA with a defined measurement window and credits. But the point of the program we’re rolling out is consistency—what engineering measures equals what product commits.

[03:39] Sarah Keane: Can you say that again but less nice? I need to know you’re not making up numbers.

[03:44] Markus Klein: Sure. The SLA is a contract. The SLO is an internal target we monitor continuously. We align them so they use the same definitions and filters. If we can’t measure it reliably, we don’t want to promise it.

[03:59] Elliot Price: And we’ll send the mapping doc that lists “SLA term” and “how we compute SLI.”

[04:07] Sarah Keane: And exclusions.

[04:09] Elliot Price: Yes, exclusions. Like invalid auth, malformed requests, customer-side timeouts, rate limited requests, that kind of thing.

[04:18] Dana Patel: Speaking of timeouts, the big one for us is streaming. We do a lot of streaming responses to a UI. If the stream drops, that’s a patient-facing issue.

[04:30] Aisha Bello: Understood. Streaming is its own reliability SLI for us. It’s not just “HTTP 200.” We track disconnects and errors on the stream.

[04:42] Miguel Alvarez: How do you differentiate a client abort versus you dropping it?

[04:47] Aisha Bello: We separate them via event taxonomy. If we see a client-side cancel signal / connection close that we can attribute to the client, that’s excluded. If the server terminates unexpectedly or there’s a gateway reset, that counts.

[05:04] Tom Nguyen: Is that consistent? Like, across regions?

[05:06] Aisha Bello: That’s part of why we’re formalizing it. Same rules across regions, and the labeling is carried in telemetry.

[05:14] Sarah Keane: Ok but if you can’t tell, what happens?

[05:18] Aisha Bello: If it’s ambiguous, we treat it conservatively in our internal reliability review. For SLA terms we’ll be explicit about what is and isn’t included. I don’t want to overcommit here without the doc in front of me.

[05:34] Markus Klein: We can follow up with exact phrasing. The overall approach is: explicit categories: invalid requests excluded, rate limiting excluded, customer abort excluded. Server-side 5xx included. Streaming server disconnect included.

[05:50] Priya Sood: From procurement: do we get monthly reporting? Or do we just trust a status page.

[05:56] Rachel Kim: For Dedicated, we generally do account-level reporting as part of the enterprise motion. And we can give you access-controlled dashboards for your account, plus a monthly summary if needed.

[06:10] Dana Patel: Access-controlled how? RBAC? SSO?

[06:13] Rachel Kim: Yes—Console supports RBAC and SSO/SAML for enterprise. Separate discussion, but yes.

[06:20] Tom Nguyen: We’ll need audit logs too.

[06:22] Markus Klein: Yep, audit logs are part of our enterprise security package. For today, we’re focusing on reliability controls.

[06:30] Aisha Bello: On the reliability side, the key is error budgets. Not just a chart. We have a policy: burn-rate alerts with multi-window thresholds, and consequences when you’re burning or you’re out.

[06:43] Dana Patel: This is the “evidence” part. Explain the consequences.

[06:48] Aisha Bello: Ok. If a tier is burning budget fast, it triggers alerts. Depending on severity, it can trigger an incident. During budget exhaustion, we can freeze non-emergency releases for that tier until we’re back in a healthy state.

[07:07] Sarah Keane: Freeze releases as in, you block deploys?

[07:10] Aisha Bello: Yes. In CI/CD we have gates. It started as warn-only, then moved toward enforcement for non-critical deploys. Emergency fixes are allowed with an override trail.

[07:24] Miguel Alvarez: That’s actually what I wanted to hear. Because otherwise it’s just “we’ll be careful.” How do you prevent someone from shipping a risky optimization when latency is already bad.

[07:34] Aisha Bello: Exactly. That’s the intent.

[07:39] Dana Patel: Can you share that policy? Like a written doc.

[07:42] Elliot Price: Yes. We can share a customer-friendly excerpt and also internal policy details under NDA if needed.

[07:51] Tom Nguyen: Also what triggers an incident. Is it when SLA is breached or SLO is burning?

[07:57] Aisha Bello: It’s tied to burn rate and user impact. We don’t wait for the monthly SLA report. If we see accelerated burn, we page.

[08:08] Rachel Kim: And from the customer side, Dedicated gets tighter expectations on comms. Meaning: you’ll get direct updates from the incident commander / comms lead, not just “check the status page.”

[08:20] Sarah Keane: That’s important. Contractually we’ll want a notice timeline. Some vendors say 72 hours which is useless.

[08:28] Rachel Kim: Understood. Typically we do initial acknowledgment quickly—like within an hour for a major issue—and then periodic updates. Exact timelines depend on severity, but we can align.

[08:41] Dana Patel: How do you handle tier-specific impact on the status page? We don’t want the public page to say “all systems operational” if Dedicated is impacted.

[08:52] Rachel Kim: We have tiered comms guidelines. Sometimes the public status page is by region and product surface. If it’s isolated to a Dedicated pool, we can do account-targeted comms and also a status page note if it’s broadly relevant. We can share the guidelines.

[09:13] Markus Klein: Also, the “tier” distinction matters: we don’t want a Hosted issue to imply your Dedicated is down, and vice versa. So the wording is careful.

[09:23] Miguel Alvarez: Let’s talk latency SLOs. Are you promising p95? p99? What endpoints.

[09:30] Aisha Bello: Internally we track p50/p95/p99 latency. SLO targets are tiered and endpoint-specific: chat/completions vs embeddings, and streaming has separate metrics.

[09:44] Miguel Alvarez: But what’s the measurement point? You said gateway receive to response complete. For streaming, response complete can be long.

[09:52] Aisha Bello: For streaming we usually split “time to first token” and “stream health.” The long tail is more about tokens/sec; we can track throughput too, but the SLO is typically about first token and disconnect rates.

[10:12] Dana Patel: I care about “the UI started responding” more than “the full thing finished.”

[10:16] Aisha Bello: Exactly. Time-to-first-token is what most customers feel.

[10:22] Sarah Keane: And what about retries and failover? If you retry behind the scenes, do you count the first failure.

[10:29] Aisha Bello: Good one. For SLI accounting, we’re careful: if we do an internal retry that succeeds, it can still count depending on whether the customer saw an error. The goal is to measure customer-perceived success and latency, while also tracking internal error rates separately.

[10:49] Miguel Alvarez: So, if you failover to a different model variant, is that a success?

[10:55] Markus Klein: Depends on policy. For Dedicated, you can choose stricter pinning. In Hosted, fallbacks are more common to preserve availability. For Dedicated, many customers want “no silent change.”

[11:09] Dana Patel: We would not want silent changes for certain workflows.

[11:12] Markus Klein: Right. We can configure fallback behavior and document it. From SLI perspective, if the request returns successfully within the agreed behavior, it’s success. But we also log “fallback occurred” as an annotation.

[11:30] Aisha Bello: And those annotations are used in incident reviews. If a fallback policy is causing customer surprise, that’s a product policy issue, not just SRE.

[11:40] Tom Nguyen: Can you provide evidence of those reviews? Like postmortems?

[11:44] Aisha Bello: We do post-incident reviews for significant incidents. We can provide redacted examples. We also have an incident process that includes IC, comms, scribe, and timelines.

[11:58] Sarah Keane: Redacted is fine as long as it shows the structure: root cause, corrective actions, owners.

[12:04] Aisha Bello: Yes.

[12:06] Markus Klein: Also, to be transparent, this quarter we’re formalizing the tiered SLO program. So the docs are actively being standardized. But the operational practice—burn-rate paging, mitigation, rollback—already exists.

[12:20] Dana Patel: That’s okay as long as you don’t hand-wave.

[12:24] Markus Klein: Totally.

[12:27] Miguel Alvarez: What happens when Dedicated and Hosted both are under stress. Who gets priority.

[12:34] Aisha Bello: Dedicated has prioritized capacity because it’s reserved. In extreme fleet constraints, we have a capacity mitigation playbook: shift traffic, add headroom, and prioritize Dedicated commitments. Hosted may shed load earlier.

[12:52] Dana Patel: Load shed meaning you return errors?

[12:55] Aisha Bello: It can mean rate-limiting or overload protection to keep the system stable. Those responses are classified clearly—rate-limited vs 5xx. Rate-limited requests are excluded from availability SLI in our definitions, but we try to avoid it for Dedicated by provisioning.

[13:16] Sarah Keane: You said “excluded.” That’s exactly what legal will fight about. If you rate limit us, we still can’t serve our users.

[13:24] Markus Klein: Yep, that’s a fair push. For Dedicated, the expectation is you have contracted capacity and we don’t rate limit you under normal usage. Rate limits are usually for Hosted tiers. For Dedicated, we’d rather do capacity planning and autoscaling within guardrails.

[13:44] Miguel Alvarez: “Within guardrails” is doing a lot of work.

[13:48] Markus Klein: Totally. That’s why we need your peak throughput numbers and regions.

[13:56] Priya Sood: Procurement needs: what is the SLA credit schedule.

[14:00] Sarah Keane: And notice obligations.

[14:03] Elliot Price: Those are in the SLA addendum templates. I can’t quote them perfectly from memory on a recorded call. But I can send the draft language and we can mark it up.

[14:14] Dana Patel: Ok, back to evidence. If our auditors ask “how do you ensure reliability improvements are prioritized,” you’ll show error budget policy + a gate, correct?

[14:26] Aisha Bello: Yes. We can show: (1) SLO dashboards, (2) burn-rate alerts tied to runbooks, (3) deploy gate behavior when a tier is red, and (4) incident artifacts.

[14:40] Tom Nguyen: Is there a monthly report output? Like a PDF or something.

[14:45] Rachel Kim: We can provide a monthly summary and give you access to the dashboard. For some customers, we do an operational review meeting.

[14:54] Miguel Alvarez: Can I see what the dashboard looks like? Not right now, but later.

[14:58] Markus Klein: Yes, we can schedule a quick walkthrough.

[15:02] Sarah Keane: I also want to understand how you define “availability.” Is it just non-5xx.

[15:09] Aisha Bello: Generally, yes: request success rate. “Success” is non-5xx for the API path, with exclusions. But streaming complicates it, which is why there’s a separate streaming reliability SLI.

[15:24] Dana Patel: So if you return 200 and then the stream dies, that’s captured.

[15:28] Aisha Bello: Yes, that’s the idea.

[15:31] Tom Nguyen: What about partial completions.

[15:34] Aisha Bello: Those are included in the streaming metric if the termination is server-side error. If it’s a client cancel, excluded.

[15:43] Miguel Alvarez: Do you have a unique request id we can give you when we open a ticket.

[15:48] Rachel Kim: Yes, request IDs are in headers and logs. For Dedicated we also can correlate to trace IDs internally.

[15:57] Dana Patel: Ok.

[16:00] (crosstalk)

[16:02] Sarah Keane: Sorry, I want to nail the incident comms. If you have a sev-1, do you notify us automatically.

[16:10] Rachel Kim: Yes, for Dedicated we’ll have an agreed distribution list / paging alias. We can do email and Slack connect in some cases. The incident bot posts internally; customer comms are curated by the comms lead.

[16:26] Dana Patel: Do you ever post on status page without telling impacted customers.

[16:31] Rachel Kim: No, not for Dedicated. If we post public, we also send direct comms. Sometimes the inverse happens: account-specific issue where we don’t post publicly, but we do direct comms.

[16:45] Tom Nguyen: That helps.

[16:47] Markus Klein: Another question we get: “how fast do you update.” Our incident process expects periodic updates; typical cadence is 30–60 minutes for ongoing sev-1, but we’ll confirm the exact expectation.

[17:04] Sarah Keane: Put it in writing.

[17:06] Rachel Kim: Yep.

[17:08] Miguel Alvarez: On the engineering side, what mitigations are allowed when budget is burning. Like do you degrade features.

[17:16] Aisha Bello: We have a runbook: traffic shaping, routing policy changes, capacity actions, rollbacks. Graceful degradation can include shedding low-priority traffic in Hosted. For Dedicated, mitigation is more often capacity + rollback + targeted routing, not “degrade output quality.”

[17:37] Markus Klein: Though there are scenarios where you might choose a fallback model variant for availability if you opt into that. But that would be a pre-agreed policy, not an ad hoc change.

[17:51] Dana Patel: We’d want to approve those policies.

[17:54] Markus Klein: Absolutely.

[18:00] Tom Nguyen: How do you demonstrate the policy is enforced. Like, can someone bypass the gate.

[18:06] Aisha Bello: There is an emergency override, but it’s logged and visible. And there’s an expectation of follow-up. We can show the existence of overrides and review.

[18:19] Sarah Keane: Good. That’s what auditors want: not “no one can ever do it,” but “there’s a trail.”

[18:26] Elliot Price: We can include that in the evidence packet.

[18:30] Dana Patel: Evidence packet sounds great. Please don’t send me 200 pages though.

[18:35] Markus Klein: We’ll keep it concise: policy excerpt, sample report, and comms template.

[18:43] Miguel Alvarez: Quick question on regions. You said regional SLOs. If EU has a problem but US doesn’t, do you report separately.

[18:51] Aisha Bello: Yes. We track per region. And for Dedicated, you’ll have region-specific dashboards.

[19:00] Rachel Kim: And in comms we’ll say “EU-West Dedicated impacted” not “all customers.”

[19:06] Dana Patel: Great.

[19:09] Sarah Keane: One more: what if the issue is a third-party cloud outage.

[19:14] Markus Klein: Usually there are force majeure / third-party exclusions in SLA language, but we can review. Operationally, we still mitigate and communicate.

[19:25] Tom Nguyen: As long as you don’t hide behind it.

[19:27] Markus Klein: Understood.

[19:30] (short pause)

[19:32] Priya Sood: Can you compare to AWS Bedrock. They just point to their SLA.

[19:38] Markus Klein: The difference is we’ll give you account-level visibility and tighter operational controls because it’s dedicated capacity with explicit SLOs and error budgets. Cloud providers often have broader, product-level metrics.

[19:54] Dana Patel: Ok.

[19:56] Miguel Alvarez: What about Azure OpenAI. We’ve seen weird streaming resets.

[20:02] Aisha Bello: Streaming reliability is a known pain point in the industry. That’s why we instrument stream errors separately and have burn-rate alerting around it.

[20:13] Dana Patel: Can you share how you classify a “stream reset.” Like is it TCP reset, or application error.

[20:21] Aisha Bello: It’s both. We bucket events: gateway disconnect, upstream reset, server exception, and client abort. Again, the doc will show the categories.

[20:35] Sarah Keane: I want that list.

[20:37] Aisha Bello: Yep.

[20:40] Markus Klein: Anything else on evidence.

[20:44] Dana Patel: The only other thing is: do you have SOC 2.

[20:47] Markus Klein: Yes, we do. But we’ll route that through the standard security package. Today we’re focusing on reliability.

[20:55] Tom Nguyen: Ok.

[20:57] Rachel Kim: Also, for escalations: we’ll give you an intake template. Timestamps, region, model, request IDs, and what you saw. It speeds up triage.

[21:09] Miguel Alvarez: Great.

[21:12] (crosstalk)

[21:14] Dana Patel: Let’s wrap with next steps.

[21:17] Markus Klein: Sure. Elliot will send the SLO-to-SLA mapping doc draft. Rachel will send incident comms guidelines and templates. Aisha will send a redacted example of an error budget burn summary and what the dashboard/report looks like.

[21:33] Rachel Kim: And you’ll confirm who receives incident notices—email distro, phone if needed, and any Slack connect preference.

[21:41] Miguel Alvarez: I’ll do that.

[21:43] Sarah Keane: And schedule the technical deep dive. I want to understand routing/fallback policy and how that ties to “success.”

[21:51] Markus Klein: Yep, I’ll set that up for next week.

[21:55] Dana Patel: Perfect.

[21:58] Tom Nguyen: Thanks.

[22:00] Markus Klein: Thanks everyone.

[Note: transcript continues with a few minutes of small talk and calendar coordination; omitted for brevity by export settings.]
